analysis.title: Global oil market tracker, Issue 23 (2 November 2026)
key_insights: ANZ classifies the oil market as 'vulnerable' on its five-pillar resilience dashboard. Most pillars sit in vulnerable territory and logistics is under severe stress, so the system has limited flexibility to absorb another shock.

Persian Gulf exports are running at 14.3mb/d, while effective throughput of oil through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to 56% of the pre-conflict normal and is trending lower. Logistics is the clearest source of stress.
ANZ assesses surplus OPEC capacity at 0mb/d under prevailing conditions. Headline spare production cannot translate into deliverable supply while export routes are impaired.

Global distillate inventories are 5.0% below their five-year average and diesel cracks have declined to USD86/bbl. Both are in vulnerable territory, pointing to persistent product scarcity despite easing margins.
Persian Gulf crude exports rebounded strongly last week after a few weeks of declines, led by higher loadings from Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
Recorded Strait of Hormuz transits remain near zero on a 7-day moving average. Dark-fleet transits fell to 1.7 vessels per day from 2 the prior week.
No crude loadings were reported at Yanbu last week, as Saudi Arabia continued to favour its east coast export system (Ras Tanura).
US crude production recovered from hurricane disruption, while US distillate and gasoline exports declined.
Crude inventories fell in Asia and the Americas and ex-China product stocks declined. Fujairah product stocks rose sharply and crude on laden vessels underway rose, while idled volumes were steady.

Global and US distillate stocks fell further, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve recorded a small drawdown of 100kbbl as the White House awarded more tenders to sell the final 40mbbl of its original 172mbbl planned release.

Dated Brent's premium to front-month futures evaporated amid stronger flows through Hormuz, while longer-dated futures rose strongly. The spread between the 1-month and Dec 27 contract rose to USD30/bbl.
Middle Eastern crude futures edged up last week while Dated Brent fell, on the prospect of indefinite disruptions to Persian Gulf flows.
Investors raised bullish Brent bets for a third consecutive week, while WTI net-long positions edged lower.

The market's expectations of fundamentals over the next 6-12 months remain at the low end of the 1.5-2.5 range (extremely tight). Crude prices appear to have moved above the level that range suggests, amid concerns about renewed hostilities.

ANZ says the 3 November US midterms are the next major geopolitical catalyst for oil. Eight months of adaptation have eroded buffers: strategic inventories are drawn down, tanker availability is tight, alternative export routes are stretched and product inventories are depleted.

ANZ sees asymmetric risk around the elections. Credible de-escalation could unwind risk premiums quickly, though depleted inventories, stronger Chinese buying and recovering demand should cushion the downside. Renewed escalation could produce a disproportionately larger price response than earlier in the conflict.

ANZ's strategy is to watch barrels, not rhetoric, after the elections. Hormuz throughput, Persian Gulf exports, tanker rates, war-risk insurance, diesel cracks and inventories are the clearest signals.

Australian fuel cover rebounded (gasoline 41 days, jet 29 days, diesel 34 days), with a 20% reduction in the minimum stockholding obligation in place for most eligible entities. Singapore inventories were little changed.

sector_views.rationale: ANZ describes the oil market as vulnerable with thin buffers, so prices are sensitive to supply, trade-flow or refinery disruptions. Risks around escalation are described as greater than the downside from de-escalation.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Exports rebounded strongly after several weeks of declines, but remain constrained by Hormuz logistics.
Trending lower. This is the clearest source of stress and limits the market's ability to redirect barrels.
Persistent product scarcity, and the deficit widened again last week.
Margins eased as government stockpile releases reduced physical tightness, but remain in vulnerable territory.
ANZ's assessment that headline spare capacity cannot reach the market while export routes are impaired.
The back of the curve is rising strongly even as the Dated Brent premium to the front month disappeared.
Down from 2 the prior week, per Rystad Energy data.

macro_indicators.indicator: US Strategic Petroleum Reserve weekly change
macro_indicators.interpretation: Small drawdown as the final 40mbbl of the original 172mbbl release is tendered.
Market expectations of fundamentals are extremely tight, and crude prices have moved above the level the index suggests.

risk_factors: Further disruption to Hormuz traffic, export infrastructure or tanker movements would hit a market with fewer options to replace lost barrels.
Renewed escalation after the US midterms, including a possible US or Israeli strike on Iran.
Attacks on Saudi refining capacity (Ras Tanura, Jazan) and continued Houthi activity.
Depleted distillate inventories and the Russian diesel export ban keep product markets tight.
Tanker availability and shipping capacity constraints, plus war-risk insurance costs.
Strategic inventories have been drawn down, including the US SPR release nearing completion.
charts_described: Dated Brent's premium to the front-month future has evaporated, while the spread between the 1-month and Dec 27 contract has risen to USD30/bbl.
Strait of Hormuz crossings: the 7-day moving averages for both outbound and inbound transits remain near zero.
Dark-fleet Hormuz transits: the 7-day moving average has fallen to 1.7 vessels per day from 2 the prior week.
US SPR: a small drawdown of 100kbbl last week.
Australian fuel cover: gasoline 41 days (+2 w/w, 97% above required volume), jet 29 days (+1 w/w, 17% above), diesel 34 days (+3 w/w, 38% above).
vol_and_positioning: Investors increased bullish Brent positions for a third consecutive week.
WTI net-long positions edged lower, and investors remain cautious in the WTI market.
The Dated Brent premium to front-month futures evaporated, while the spread between the 1-month and Dec 27 contract widened to USD30/bbl.
geopolitical: Iranian negotiators are in Doha for talks with Qatari mediators aimed at a deal to end the war between the US and Iran, per Reuters.
Axios reported that Prime Minister Netanyahu is pressing President Trump to strike Iran immediately after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The US Navy warned last week that vessels should avoid the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman unless transit is necessary.
Houthis said they attacked the 550kb/d Ras Tanura refinery last week, and the 400kb/d Jazan refinery is expected to be offline through Q4 2026.
Russia extended a general diesel export ban to the end of January, despite a deal with the US to release Russian diesel back onto the international market.
OPEC reaffirmed plans to keep output quotas unchanged in December, with supply curbed by the Middle East conflict.

tension_points.theme: oil risk premium around US midterms
tension_points.bull_case: Renewed escalation would hit a market with depleted inventories, constrained shipping and 0mb/d deliverable OPEC spare capacity, so the price response could be disproportionately larger than earlier in the conflict.
tension_points.bear_case: A credible de-escalation could see geopolitical risk premiums unwind quickly, though depleted inventories, stronger Chinese buying and recovering demand should cushion the downside.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A deterioration in physical flows (Hormuz throughput, Persian Gulf exports, tanker rates, war-risk insurance, diesel cracks, inventories) would confirm the tightening. Improvement in those flows would weaken it.

theme_stances.key_argument: Buffers are eroded and logistics are under severe stress, so the market has limited ability to absorb another supply shock.
Risks around the US elections are asymmetric, with renewed escalation posing the greater risk to prices.
theme_stances.evidence: Renewed escalation poses a greater risk.
